result.summary: An editorial note dates the ode to Psaumis' mule-chariot victory at Olympia in 452 B.C. The poet then invokes Zeus, presents the victory song, praises Psaumis, and begins a myth of Erginos, son of Klymenos, who won the Lemnian race in bronze armour.

scenes.title: Editor's introductory note
scenes.summary: The editor dates the ode, explains the mule-chariot race, and describes how the ode was probably sung that night.

scenes.title: Hymn to Zeus and praise
scenes.summary: The poet calls on Zeus to receive the victory song and praises Psaumis for horse-rearing, hospitality and civic peace. He introduces a tale proving that trial tests men.
scenes.stakes: Psaumis' glory and Kamarina's honour depend on the god's favour and the song's truthful praise.

scenes.title: Son of Klymenos on Lemnos
scenes.summary: After winning the armoured foot-race, the son of Klymenos tells Hypsipyle that his hands and heart match his speed, and that young men can have grey hair.
scenes.stakes: His reputation among the Lemnian women who had slighted him.

alias_notes.explanation: The ode does not name him; tradition identifies him as Erginos.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable statement of the ode's moral that trial tests men.

analysis.text: The ode joins victory, divine favour and truthful praise, using the Lemnian myth to show that proof comes through trial.
Mule-chariot races were run at Olympia only from 500 to 444 B.C., and this ode is among Pindar's latest datable work.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias is the source cited for the brief life of the mule-chariot race at Olympia.

language_notes.text: "Thy chosen hour recurrent" means the festival season that returns at its appointed time; the poet is sent by Zeus's recurring festival.
Typhon was a hundred-headed monster said to be pinned beneath Ætna by Zeus; the "wind-beaten burden" is the mountain itself.
"Good hap" means good fortune; "forthwith" means immediately.
"Pisan olive" refers to the wild-olive crown given at Olympia, which lay in the territory of Pisa.
The Lemnian women had killed their husbands and slighted the Argonauts' men; the son of Klymenos (Erginos) was mocked by them for his grey hair before winning the race.
Hypsipyle was queen of Lemnos; the race was held there in her honour, with prizes of cloaks.

context_notes.text: Pausanias was a Greek travel writer of the 2nd century A.D. who described Olympia and its history.
Zeus, son of Kronos, was king of the gods and patron of the Olympic games.
Kamarina was a Greek city in Sicily, Psaumis' home.

literary_notes.text: The poet addresses Zeus directly, opening the ode as a prayer and making the victory song an offering to the god.
The compact saying "trial is the test of men" states the ode's theme and introduces the myth as proof.
Grey hairs on young men reverses the expectation that age brings slowness; the boast shows that appearance misleads about prowess.
